content.title: Predicting Experimental Results After Variable Changes
content.overview: This lesson teaches how to predict the outcome of a hypothetical experiment by isolating the effect of a single variable change and applying that change to a known baseline trial.
learning_objectives: Identify the baseline trial that matches the fixed variables of a hypothetical scenario.
Calculate the isolated effect size of a single variable change using existing data.
Apply the isolated effect to a baseline result to predict a new experimental outcome.
Verify the consistency of a predicted change across multiple trial pairs.

sections.title: The Isolate-and-Apply Strategy
sections.content:
When the ACT asks you to predict a result after changing one variable, you must use the 'Isolate-and-Apply' strategy. First, identify the baseline trial—this is the trial in the data table where all variables match your target scenario except for the one being changed. Second, determine the isolated effect, which is the numerical difference in the outcome caused by changing only that specific variable. Finally, apply that difference to your baseline result to find the new predicted value.

![A flowchart showing the steps: Identify Baseline, Isolate Effect, Apply to Baseline, and Verify Consistency.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/f3d22ab1-7fbe-4717-bea2-ba27265a95be-1786506685891-576.webp)

sections.title: Identifying the Baseline and Effect Size
sections.content: A baseline trial is a recorded data point whose conditions match the 'fixed' variables in the question. To find the effect size, look for two existing trials that differ only by the variable you are investigating. For example, if you are changing temperature from 20°C to 30°C, find two trials where all other factors (pressure, volume, etc.) are identical, and subtract their results to see how much the 10-degree increase changed the outcome.

sections.title: The Additive Assumption
sections.content: In most ACT Science passages, we use the additive assumption. This assumes that the isolated effect of a variable remains constant regardless of the other conditions, unless the data explicitly shows a non-linear relationship or an interaction. If changing light intensity adds 5cm of growth at one water level, we assume it will add 5cm at a different water level unless the table proves otherwise.

worked_examples.question: A study measures seedling height under two light levels (Low/High) and two water volumes (50mL/100mL). Data: [Low light, 50mL = 6cm], [Low light, 100mL = 9cm], [High light, 50mL = 12cm], [High light, 100mL = 15cm]. Predict the height if a seedling is grown under High light with 50mL of water, starting from the Low light/50mL baseline.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the baseline. The question asks for High light at 50mL. The baseline with the same water volume (50mL) but the original light level (Low) is 6cm. Step 2: Isolate the effect of light. Compare Low light/50mL (6cm) to High light/50mL (12cm). The change from Low to High light results in a +6cm increase. Step 3: Apply the effect. Baseline (6cm) + Effect (+6cm) = 12cm. Verification: Check the 100mL trials. High light/100mL (15cm) minus Low light/100mL (9cm) also equals +6cm, confirming the effect is consistent.

common_mistakes: Adding multiple effects: Mistakenly adding the changes of two different variables when the question only asks for the change of one.
Wrong Baseline: Selecting a trial where the 'fixed' variables do not match the hypothetical scenario.
Directional Error: Subtracting an effect that should be added, or vice versa (e.g., ignoring that a variable decrease might lead to a result increase).
exam_tips: Always double-check the units in the table versus the units in the question to ensure they match.
If the data shows a trend (e.g., doubling the variable doubles the result), use that ratio to predict values outside the table.
Quickly scan other trial pairs to ensure the 'effect size' you calculated is consistent throughout the experiment.
content.recap: To predict a new result, find a baseline trial that matches your fixed conditions, calculate the numerical impact of the variable being changed from other trials, and apply that impact to the baseline.

knowledge_claims.content: A baseline trial is a recorded trial where all conditions match the fixed (unchanged) variables of a hypothetical scenario.
To predict a result after changing one variable, first identify the baseline trial and then isolate the effect size of the target variable.
Isolated effect is the measured difference in outcome between two trials that differ by only one variable.
The additive assumption implies that an isolated effect applies consistently to a baseline unless the data demonstrates a non-linear interaction.
Verification of a prediction involves checking if the same variable change produces the same effect size in other pairs of trials in the data set.
A common error is adding the effects of two variables when the question specifies that only one variable is being changed.
Recognizing the baseline requires matching the values of all variables that the question states will 'stay the same' or 'remain fixed'.
If a variable change from 10 to 20 units increases the result by 5, applying this effect to a baseline of 15 results in a predicted value of 20.
When predicting results, the direction of the change (increase vs. decrease) must match the observed trend in the provided trials.
Comparing two trials that differ by only one variable allows a researcher to quantify the specific impact of that variable on the dependent measurement.
The final step in the Isolate-and-Apply strategy is to add or subtract the isolated effect from the baseline trial's measured result.
If doubling a variable doubles the outcome in existing trials, this proportional relationship should be used for predictions involving that variable.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 6: Origins of Bright Crater Rays
Three students discuss why some young impact craters have bright rays extending across the surface.

Student 1: The rays consist mainly of fresh material excavated from beneath a dark, weathered surface. With time, exposure to radiation and tiny impacts darkens the rays until they resemble the surrounding ground.

Student 2: The material is not intrinsically brighter. Impact fragments roughen the surface, and the rough texture reflects sunlight toward the observer at certain angles. As small grains settle, the directional reflection weakens.

Student 3: Both excavation and texture matter. Fresh subsurface material begins brighter than the surface, and rough fragment deposits enhance that contrast. Weathering and settling therefore work together to fade the rays.

Which investigation would best distinguish the proposed explanations?

options.F: Ask one observer which explanation sounds most familiar.
options.G: Measure only the final outcome without varying or comparing any relevant factor.
options.H: Measure both composition and reflectance at several viewing angles for ray and non-ray material.
options.J: Remove all records of the procedures before interpreting the results.

items.explanation: The proposed test measures variables that differ among the explanations.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 2: Mulch and Soil Infiltration
Students packed identical soil columns and applied simulated rain. Experiment 1 compared bare soil with 2 cm and 5 cm layers of straw mulch. They measured water collected below each column after 20 minutes. Experiment 2 repeated the treatments after gently compacting the soil.

Which factor was held constant and therefore helped make treatment comparisons meaningful?

options.C: the conclusion written after the experiment
options.D: soil mass, rainfall rate, and collection time

items.explanation: A controlled factor is kept the same across conditions so differences can be attributed more confidently.

videoLesson.title: Predict Outcome From Single-Variable Change
videoLesson.description: Recognize the baseline trial with matching variables and its measured result. Isolate the variable’s effect from paired trials and add or subtract that change to predict the new value.
